messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Reyes is a 24-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment months after surviving a bombing at a crowded bus terminal on her way home from an evening shift. She remembers the compressed details more than any whole sequence: the crush of bodies in line, a sharp metallic crack she first took for something dropped, and then the force of the blast throwing people sideways. What stayed with her most was movement—arms jerking up, strangers lunging, people running without direction. The scene is broken in her mind. There are stretches she cannot account for at all, and when she tries to explain what happened, she stops in frustration, saying she knows it happened but cannot find words that feel big enough or precise enough. At other moments the memory returns with a surge of rage so sudden it feels almost physical, especially when she thinks about how ordinary the night had seemed before everything changed.

In the weeks after, Marisol had come to believe that the world was simply dangerous now, not in an abstract sense but everywhere and all the time. She was certain that safety depended on staying alert because danger could break through without warning. Just as unsettling, her body no longer felt reliable to her. She hated how it jumped before she could think, how it seemed to react on its own, and this made her feel she had to monitor herself as closely as she monitored everyone else. From there, being on guard ceased to feel like a choice and began to feel like the only responsible way to move through the day. At the warehouse she now tracks every forklift turn, every coworker stepping suddenly out from behind stacked pallets, every dropped box. She avoids eye contact on the floor because meeting someone’s gaze leaves her feeling exposed and distractible, and she keeps scanning aisles, exits, and doorways instead.

That constant sense of danger has sharpened into a physical threat response that governs much of her life. Sudden movements by other people put her immediately on guard; even a coworker reaching quickly for a scanner can make her flinch and tense. She is jumpy in general, and nights are especially difficult. Since the bombing happened after dark, evening brings a particular feeling that the world is less controllable, as if threats are harder to detect and more likely to arrive fast. When she leaves late shifts, she checks parking areas and the street repeatedly, watching hands, body positions, and who is moving toward her. Because she feels keyed up so often, she has begun to rely even more on scanning her surroundings constantly, as though relaxing for a second would be the moment she misses something vital.

Her fractured memory also feeds these habits. The gaps are intolerable to her; not knowing exactly what happened makes her feel unprepared, as if the missing pieces contain some warning she failed to notice. When images or sensations from that night break through and she cannot put them into words, she sometimes deliberately tries to blank out, going mentally distant to escape both the helplessness of not remembering and the anger that comes with remembering too much. During breaks at work, if a noise in the loading bay or a rush of bodies at shift change stirs the scene at the terminal, she can feel herself pulling away inside, staring past people rather than at them. Those same broken, wordless fragments also keep her body on edge; a burst of motion around her can feel dangerous before she even knows why, as if the memory is being carried in reflex rather than thought.

Over time, the ways Marisol has tried to protect herself have deepened the beliefs she already holds. Constant scanning makes every setting feel full of possible threat, because there is always another movement to track or another person to watch. Avoiding eye contact leaves other people seeming less readable and more unpredictable, which confirms her sense that the world is unsafe. Deliberately blanking out gives brief relief, but afterward she feels even less able to trust her own body and mind, disturbed by how easily she can disappear from herself. When her startle response fires or she finds herself most vigilant at night, it seems to prove that her danger is ongoing rather than past. And when she reacts this way, the event remains not fully settled in memory but raw, fragmented, and rage-filled, with the unspeakable parts still looming.

What finally brought her in was a recent incident at work when a pallet shifted and a coworker grabbed her arm quickly to steady her. Marisol jerked away so hard that she nearly fell, then went blank for several seconds and could not answer when he asked if she was okay. She was humiliated afterward and frightened by how automatic it felt. She is seeking help now because she is tired of living as if every movement around her might be the start of another attack, and because what frightens her most is the thought that she may never again be able to trust either the world outside her or the body she has to live in.
